Sectional monodromy groups of projective curvesThanks: This research was supported in part by Simons Foundation grant #402472 (to Bjorn Poonen)

Borys Kadets Address: Department of Mathematics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139-4307, USA Email address: bkadets@mit.edu URL: http://math.mit.edu/~bkadets/
Abstract.

Fix a degree dd projective curve X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} over an algebraically closed field KK. Let U⊂(ℙr)∗U\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} be a dense open subvariety such that every hyperplane H∈UH\in U intersects XX in dd smooth points. Varying H∈UH\in U produces the monodromy action φ:π1ét​(U)→Sd\varphi:\pi_{1}^{{\text{\'{e}t}}}(U)\to S_{d}. Let GX:⁣=im(φ)G_{X}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\im(\varphi). The permutation group GXG_{X} is called the sectional monodromy group of XX. In characteristic zero GXG_{X} is always the full symmetric group, but sectional monodromy groups in characteristic pp can be smaller. For a large class of space curves (r⩾3r\geqslant 3) we classify all possibilities for the sectional monodromy group GG as well as the curves with GX=GG_{X}=G. We apply similar methods to study a particular family of rational curves in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}, which enables us to answer an old question about Galois groups of generic trinomials.

14H50, 14E20, 12F10

1. Introduction

Let KK be an algebraically closed field. Consider an integral nondegenerate proper curve XX in the projective space ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} over KK. Choose coordinates x0,…,xrx_{0},...,x_{r} on ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r}. Extend scalars from KK to L=K⁡(t1,…,tr)L=K(t_{1},...,t_{r}) and consider the subscheme Z⊂ℙLrZ\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}_{L} given by the intersection of XLX_{L} with the hyperplane x0+t1​x1+…+tr​xr=0x_{0}+t_{1}x_{1}+...+t_{r}x_{r}=0. The scheme ZZ is the spectrum of a finite separable extension MM of LL (see Lemma 2.1). The Galois group GG of the Galois closure of MM over LL is our main object of interest and will be referred to as the sectional monodromy group. One can think of GG geometrically as the monodromy of the hyperplane section H∩XH\cap X as the hyperplane HH varies. A folklore result is the following.

Proposition 1.1 (see Remark 3.5).

Assume that the characteristic of KK is zero. Let dd be the degree of XX. Then G≅SdG\cong S_{d}.

The result is important in the study of curves in projective space. For instance, it can be used to restrict the possibilities for Hilbert polynomials of space curves; for more details see [Harris1980], [Eisenbud-Harris1982].

The char⁡K=0\Char K=0 assumption of Proposition 1.1 cannot be removed. For example, when char⁡K=p\Char K=p, the sectional monodromy group of the rational plane curve xp=y​zp−1x^{p}=yz^{p-1} is AGL1⁡(p)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(p).

Motivated by geometric applications, Rathmann [Rathmann1987] proved a version of Proposition 1.1 valid in all characteristics.

Theorem 1.2 (Rathmann).

Assume that X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} is a smooth nondegenerate curve of degree dd. Assume r⩾4r\geqslant 4. Then the sectional monodromy group of XX contains the alternating group AdA_{d}.

Remark 1.3.

Gareth Jones noticed that Rathmann’s paper [Rathmann1987] contains a group-theoretic error: the list of triply transitive groups in [Rathmann1987]*Theorem 2.4 is incomplete. It is unclear if this gap is easy to fix. For instance, one of the omitted Mathieu groups Aut⁡(M22)\Aut(M_{22}) is not contained in the alternating group, so the proof of [Rathmann1987]*Proposition 2.14 requires a separate analysis of this case.

Rathmann also gave an example of a smooth rational curve in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} with G=PGL2⁡(q)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(q). Rathmann’s theorem is important for understanding statistics over function fields, for example the large characteristic version of the Bateman-Horn conjecture (see [Entin-preprint]*Section 6 for examples of such statistical problems). In Section 3 we prove an extension of Rathmann’s theorem that applies to nonsmooth curves in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3}. Recall that a projective curve is called strange if all of its tangent lines pass through a common point. Strange curves are rare, for example the only smooth strange curves are lines in any characteristic and conics in characteristic 22. The tangent variety of XX (also called the tangent developable surface) is the Zariski closure of the union of lines tangent to XX.

Theorem 1.4.

Assume X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} is an integral nondegenerate curve of degree dd. Assume that r⩾3r\geqslant 3 and XX is not strange. Then exactly one of the following is true.

  1. (1)

    The sectional monodromy group of XX contains AdA_{d}.

  2. (2)

    r=3r=3 and the curve XX is projectively equivalent to the projective closure of the rational curve {(t,tq,tq+1),t∈K}⊂𝔸K3\{(t,t^{q},t^{q+1}),t\in K\}\subset\mathbb{A}_{K}^{3} for some power qq of the characteristic. The sectional monodromy group of XX is PGL2⁡(q)\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(q).

  3. (3)

    r=3r=3, char⁡K=2\Char K=2, the tangent variety of XX is a smooth quadric and G⊂AGLn⁡(2)G\subset\operatorname{AGL}_{n}(2).

Note that the curves that satisfy the assumptions of Theorem 1.4 and have small sectional monodromy groups are either rational or contained in a smooth quadric. Rational curves and curves lying on quadrics are not important for the applications to the degree-genus problem.

For plane curves, sectional monodromy groups are not known even in the following very simple case.

Example 1.5.

Let Xn,mX_{n,m} be the rational curve xn=ym​zn−mx^{n}=y^{m}z^{n-m} for some relatively prime integers n>m>0n>m>0. Then the sectional monodromy group of XX is the Galois group of the trinomial xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b over K⁡(a,b)K(a,b). Classifying possible Galois groups of generic trinomials is an old problem; see [Cohen1980], [Smith1977], [Uchida1970], [Smith1984]. A closely related problem of classifying Galois groups of trinomials over the function field K⁡(t)K(t) when aa and bb are specialized to powers of tt has also been widely studied; see [Abhyankar1992], [Abhyankar1993], [Abhyankar1993.2], [Abhyankar1994], [Abhyankar-Seiler-Popp1992], [Conway-et-al2010].

The curves Xm,nX_{m,n} do not satisfy both of the assumptions of Theorem 1.4: they are evidently plane curves (r=2r=2) and many of them are strange. Nevertheless, we can use methods similar to those in the proof of Theorem 1.4 to study the curves Xm,nX_{m,n}. In section 5 we prove the following theorem.

Theorem 1.6.

Let KK be an algebraically closed field of characteristic pp. Let n,mn,m be a pair of relatively prime integers with m<nm<n. Let GG be the Galois group of the polynomial xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b over K⁡(a,b)K(a,b).

  1. (1)

    If n=pdn=p^{d} and m=1m=1 or m=pd−1m=p^{d}-1, then G=AGL1⁡(pd)G=\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(p^{d}).

  2. (2)

    If n=6n=6, m=1m=1 or m=5m=5, and p=2p=2, then G=PSL2⁡(5)G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(5).

  3. (3)

    If n=12n=12, m=1m=1 or m=11m=11, and p=3p=3, then G=M11G=M_{11} (a Mathieu group, see [Conway1999]).

  4. (4)

    If n=24n=24, m=1m=1 or m=23m=23, and p=2p=2, then G=M24G=M_{24}.

  5. (5)

    If n=11n=11, m=2m=2 or m=9m=9, and p=3p=3, then G=M11G=M_{11}.

  6. (6)

    If n=23n=23, m=3m=3 or m=20m=20, and p=2p=2, then G=M23G=M_{23}.

  7. (7)

    Let q:⁣=pkq\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}p^{k} for some integer kk. If n=(qd−1)/(q−1)n=(q^{d}-1)/(q-1), m=(qs−1)/(q−1)m=(q^{s}-1)/(q-1) or m=n−(qs−1)/(q−1)m=n-(q^{s}-1)/(q-1) for some integers s,ds,d, then G=PGLd⁡(q)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{d}(q).

  8. (8)

    If none of the above holds, then An⊂GA_{n}\subset G.

BWarning. The aforementioned result of Rathmann as well as the results of this paper depend on the classification of finite simple groups.

2. Transitivity of Sectional Monodromy Groups

From now on, let KK denote a fixed algebraically closed field. We first give a more geometric definition of the sectional monodromy groups from the introduction. Let r⩾2r\geqslant 2 be an integer and let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} be a degree dd projective nondegenerate integral curve. Consider the incidence scheme I=IX⊂X×(ℙr)∗I=I_{X}\subset X\times(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} parameterizing pairs (P,H)(P,H) of points P∈XP\in X and hyperplanes H⊂ℙrH\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} subject to the condition P∈HP\in H. The scheme ZZ from the introduction is the generic fiber of the projection π=πX:IX→(ℙr)∗.\pi=\pi_{X}\colon I_{X}\to(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*}. We call the covering πX\pi_{X} the sectional covering associated to XX.

Lemma 2.1.

The incidence scheme II is irreducible. The morphism π\pi is finite of degree dd and generically étale.

Proof.

The fibers of the first coordinate projection I→XI\to X are projective spaces of dimension r−1r-1; hence II is irreducible. The morphism is generically étale by Bertini’s theorem [Jouanolou1983]*Proposition 6.4, and finite since it is quasi-finite and proper. ∎

Lemma 2.1 implies that the sectional monodromy group GG is well-defined and acts transitively on a set of dd points. If U⊂(ℙr)∗U\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} is a dense open subset over which π\pi is étale and Ω\Omega is a fiber of π\pi over a geometric point of UU, then GG can be identified with the image of π1ét​(U)\pi_{1}^{{\text{\'{e}t}}}(U) in Sym⁡(Ω)\mathrm{Sym}(\Omega). If Z⊂UZ\subset U is a closed subset, then the monodromy group of π−1​(Z)→Z\pi^{-1}(Z)\to Z is a permutation subgroup of GG. We now show that the action of GG on Ω\Omega is always 2-transitive, and has even higher transitivity degree if the curve is not “strange”.

Lemma 2.2.

The sectional monodromy group acts doubly transitively.

Proof.

Choose a hyperplane HH that intersects XX at dd distinct smooth points. Let PP be one of the points in H∩XH\cap X. Choose an (r−2)(r-2)-dimensional subspace VV in ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} such that V∩X=PV\cap X=P. Consider the line l⊂(ℙr)∗l\subset(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} corresponding to the family of hyperplanes containing VV. Let Z=π−1​(l)Z=\pi^{-1}(l). Projection of ZZ to XX is an isomorphism over X∖PX\setminus P. The fiber above PP is isomorphic to ll (via π\pi). Therefore ZZ decomposes into a union of two irreducible components Z=Z1∪Z2Z=Z_{1}\cup Z_{2}, where π:Z1→l\pi\colon Z_{1}\to l is an isomorphism and Z2Z_{2} is isomorphic to XX. Since the fiber of π′=π|Z2:Z2→l\pi^{\prime}=\pi|_{Z_{2}}\colon Z_{2}\to l above the point of ll corresponding to HH is smooth, the covering π′\pi^{\prime} is generically étale. Therefore, the monodromy group GG contains a subgroup that acts via fixing one point and acting transitively on the others. Thus GG is doubly transitive. ∎

For every rr there are examples of integral nondegenerate curves X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} for which GXG_{X} is not triply transitive (see [Rathmann1987]*Example 1.2). However we will prove that GXG_{X} is rr-transitive if XX is not “strange”. We recall the definition of a strange curve.

Definition 2.3.

An integral curve XX in ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} is called strange if the tangent lines to XX at the smooth points pass through a common point.

Remark 2.4.

Equivalently, an integral curve is strange if the tangent lines to XX at all but finitely many smooth points pass through a common point.

A secant of a curve XX is a line intersecting it in at least 22 points.

Proposition 2.5.

If every secant intersects XX in at least three points, then XX is strange.

Proof.

See [Hartshorne1977]*Proposition 3.3.8. ∎

Most of the results that follow concern curves that are not strange. It is natural to expect higher transitivity for nonstrange curves. This is the case, as we show in Proposition 2.8. We precede the proof of Proposition 2.8 with two lemmas.

Lemma 2.6.

Let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}, r⩾3r\geqslant 3 be a proper nondegenerate nonstrange integral curve. Let ℒ\mathcal{L} denote the set of lines in ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} that have nonempty intersection with every tangent to XX. Then either ℒ\mathcal{L} is finite or r=3r=3, XX is contained in a smooth quadric, and ℒ\mathcal{L} is one of the quadric’s rulings.

Proof.

Assume that ℒ\mathcal{L} is infinite. Consider two distinct lines ℓ1,ℓ2∈ℒ\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\in\mathcal{L}. If ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2} intersect, then either every tangent to XX passes through ℓ1∩ℓ2\ell_{1}\cap\ell_{2} or every tangent to XX is in the plane containing ℓ1\ell_{1} and ℓ2\ell_{2}. Since XX is nondegenerate and nonstrange, neither of these is possible. Therefore any two distinct lines from ℒ\mathcal{L} are skew. Consider two skew lines ℓ1,ℓ2∈ℒ\ell_{1},\ell_{2}\in\mathcal{L}. Since every tangent of XX crosses both of them, the curve XX lies in the dimension three projective subspace of ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} that contains ℓ1,ℓ2\ell_{1},\ell_{2}. Hence r=3r=3. A classical fact, which we prove below, is that the union of lines that intersect three pairwise skew lines is a smooth quadric. Thus there exists a smooth quadric QQ containing every tangent line of XX. Elements of ℒ\mathcal{L} are pairwise skew and lie on QQ, therefore ℒ\mathcal{L} forms one of the rulings of QQ.

We now show that the union of lines intersecting three fixed lines in ℙ3\mathbb{P}^{3} is a smooth quadric. Since 10=dimH0​(ℙ3,𝒪⁡(2))>3​dimH0​(ℙ1,𝒪⁡(2))=910=\dim H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{3},\mathcal{O}(2))>3\dim H^{0}(\mathbb{P}^{1},\mathcal{O}(2))=9, there exists a quadric containing any triple of lines. If the lines are pairwise skew, the quadric cannot be a cone or a pair of planes; therefore it must be smooth. Every line intersecting a smooth quadric in at least three points has to lie on it. ∎

Lemma 2.7.

Let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}, r⩾3r\geqslant 3 be a nonstrange nondegenerate integral curve. If r=3r=3 assume additionaly that XX is not contained in a quadric. Then the projection from a general point PP of XX is birational onto its image. Moreover, the image of a general projection is nonstrange.

Proof.

Consider the set ℒ\mathcal{L} of Lemma 2.6. Since XX is not contained in a quadric, ℒ\mathcal{L} is finite. Proposition 2.5 implies that a general point of XX lies on finitely many multisecants. Therefore projection from a general point is generically one-to-one on KK points and is thus birational. Let P∈X⁡(K)P\in X(K) be a point such that the projection πP:X→Y\pi_{P}\colon X\to Y from PP is birational onto its image YY, and such that PP does not lie on a line from ℒ\mathcal{L}. Suppose that YY is strange and all the tangents pass through Q∈ℙr−1Q\in\mathbb{P}^{r-1}. Then the line πP−1​(Q)⊂ℙr\pi_{P}^{-1}(Q)\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} is an element of ℒ\mathcal{L} that contains PP. Thus YY is nonstrange.

∎

Proposition 2.8.

If X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}, r⩾2r\geqslant 2 is an integral nondegenerate nonstrange curve, then GG is rr-transitive.

Proof.

We prove the statement by induction on rr. The case r=2r=2 is Lemma 2.2. Assume r>2r>2. Assume first that it is not the case that r=3r=3 and XX lies on a quadric. Choose a point P∈X⁡(K)P\in X(K) such that the conclusions of Lemma 2.7 hold. Let Y⊂ℙr−1Y\subset\mathbb{P}^{r-1} be the projection of XX from PP. Consider the hyperplane H∈(ℙr)∗H\in(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} corresponding to the family of hyperplanes in ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} passing through PP. Let ZZ denote π−1​(H)\pi^{-1}(H). The scheme ZZ has an irreducible component Z′=P×H⊂X×(ℙr)∗Z^{\prime}=P\times H\subset X\times(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*}. The covering Z∖Z′→HZ\setminus Z^{\prime}\to H is birational to the sectional covering of YY, since the preimages of hyperplanes in ℙr−1\mathbb{P}^{r-1} are hyperplanes in ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r} containing PP. By the induction hypothesis the monodromy group of the covering Z∖Z′→HZ\setminus Z^{\prime}\to H is r−1r-1-transitive. The covering Z′→HZ^{\prime}\to H is an isomorphism. Therefore the monodromy group of Z→HZ\to H acts by fixing one point and acting (r−1)(r-1)-transitively on the rest. Since GG acts transitively and contains a subgroup acting (r−1)(r-1)-transitively on all but one (fixed) point, GG is rr-transitive.

We have to show that when r=3r=3 and XX lies on a quadric QQ the group is 33-transitive. Consider a generic plane HH. We can assume that both H∩XH\cap X and H∩QH\cap Q are smooth. Take two points of H∩XH\cap X and a line ℓ\ell through them. The line ℓ\ell contains exactly two points P1,P2P_{1},P_{2} of the curve. Consider the line ℓ∗∈(ℙ3)∗\ell^{*}\in(\mathbb{P}^{3})^{*} corresponding to the hyperplanes containing ℓ\ell. The restriction of the sectional covering of XX to ℓ∗\ell^{*} is generically étale since H∩XH\cap X is smooth. Let Y⊂X×ℓ∗Y\subset X\times\ell^{*} denote the preimage of ℓ\ell under πX\pi_{X}. The projection of YY to XX is an isomorphism over X∖{P1,P2}X\setminus\{P_{1},P_{2}\}. The preimages of P1P_{1}, P2P_{2} in YY are each isomorphic to ℓ∗\ell^{*}. Therefore YY decomposes into a union of irreducible components Y=Y1​⋃Y2​⋃Y3Y=Y_{1}\bigcup Y_{2}\bigcup Y_{3}, where Y1Y_{1} is isomorphic to XX and Y2,Y3Y_{2},Y_{3} are isomorphic to ℓ∗\ell^{*}. Hence the monodromy group contains a subgroup that acts by fixing two points and acting transitively on the rest. Therefore GG is triply transitive. ∎

Multiple transitivity is a very strong condition on the group. For example, the only 55-transitive groups are AnA_{n} and SnS_{n} in their natural actions and the Mathieu groups M12M_{12} and M24M_{24} acting on 1212 and 2424 points respectively. The classification of 22-transitive groups is known; see, for example, [Dixon-Mortimer1996]*§7.7 for the statement.

Remark 2.9.

It is common to state classification results on permutation groups without specifying the action (or by referring to the “natural” action). This is relatively harmless except for the cases of M11M_{11}, which has two multiply-transitive actions on 1111 and 1212 points, and of M12M_{12}, which has two multiply transitive actions on 1212 points exchanged by an outer automorphism.

The following proposition due to Rathmann describes the behavior of the sectional monodromy group with respect to projections from points outside of the curve.

Proposition 2.10 ([Rathmann1987]*Proposition 1.10.).

Let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}, r⩾3r\geqslant 3 be a projective nondegenerate integral curve. Let YY be the projection of XX from a general point of ℙr\mathbb{P}^{r}. Then the sectional monodromy groups of XX and YY are isomorphic.

3. Tangents and inertia groups

We will compute sectional monodromy groups by restricting the sectional monodromy covering πX\pi_{X} to a line in (ℙr)∗(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} and computing inertia groups. A natural choice of a point in (ℙr)∗(\mathbb{P}^{r})^{*} above which the restricted covering ramifies is a point corresponding to a hyperplane containing a tangent line of XX. Tangent hyperplanes can behave pathologically in characteristic pp (even for nonstrange curves).

For the statements and precise definitions in this paragraph see [Hefez1989] and references therein. Let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r} be an integral projective curve that is not a line. The dual curve X∗⊂Gr⁡(2,r+1)X^{*}\subset\mathrm{Gr}(2,r+1) is defined to be the closure of the set of tangent lines to XX. The Gauss map is the rational map γ:X⇢X∗\upgamma:X\dashrightarrow X^{*} that sends a point to the tangent line at that point. In characteristic 00 the Gauss map is birational. In characteristic pp both the separable degree ss and the inseparable degree qq of γ\upgamma can be greater than one. A general tangent line of XX has ss points of tangency with multiplicity max⁡(q,2)\max(q,2) at each one. It is a theorem of Kaji that Gauss maps can be arbitrary bad in the sense that any finite inseparable extension of function fields can be realized as the generic fiber of a Gauss map; see [Kaji1989]*Corollary 3.4.

We calculate inertia groups by computing Galois groups of certain extensions of K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)} given by adjoining to K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)} zeros of convergent power series of a specific shape. Our main tool is the theory of Newton polygons (see [Koblitz1984]*IV.4) that determines the valuations of the roots of a power series from the valuations of its coefficients. We combine the information obtained from Newton polygons with basic ramification theory to determine the local Galois groups; for an introduction to ramification theory see [SerreLocalFields1979]*Chapters I–III.

We will use the following group theoretic result due to Jones [Jones2014]. Recall that a permutation group GG acting on Ω\Omega is primitive if it preserves no nontrivial partition of Ω\Omega.

Theorem 3.1 (Jones).

Let GG be a primitive permutation group of finite degree nn, not containing AnA_{n}. Suppose that GG contains a cycle fixing exactly kk points, where 0⩽k⩽n−20\leqslant k\leqslant n-2. Then one of the following holds:

  1. (1)

    k=0k=0 and either

    1. (1)

      Cp⊂G⊂AGL1⁡(p)C_{p}\subset G\subset\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(p) with n=pn=p prime, or

    2. (2)

      PGLd⁡(q)⊂G⊂P​Γ​Ld⁡(q)\operatorname{PGL}_{d}(q)\subset G\subset\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_{d}(q) with n=(qd−1)/(q−1)n=(q^{d}-1)/(q-1) and d⩾2d\geqslant 2 for some prime power qq, or

    3. (3)

      G=PSL2⁡(11),M11G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(11),M_{11} or M23M_{23} with n=11,11,23n=11,11,23 respectively.

  2. (2)

    k=1k=1 and either

    1. (1)

      AGLd⁡(q)⊂G⊂A​Γ​Ld⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{d}(q)\subset G\subset\operatorname{A\Gamma L}_{d}(q) with n=qdn=q^{d} and d⩾1d\geqslant 1 for some prime power qq, or

    2. (2)

      G=PSL2⁡(p)G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(p) or G=PGL2⁡(p)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(p) with n=p+1n=p+1 for some prime p⩾5p\geqslant 5, or

    3. (3)

      G=M11,M12G=M_{11},M_{12} or M24M_{24} with n=12,12,24n=12,12,24 respectively. respectively.

  3. (3)

    k=2k=2 and PGL2⁡(q)⊂G⊂P​Γ​L2⁡(q)\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(q)\subset G\subset\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_{2}(q) with n=q+1n=q+1 for some prime power qq.

The inclusions in Theorem 3.1 are inclusions of permutation groups. We recall the definitions of some of the groups appearing in Theorem 3.1. The group AGLd⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{d}(q) is the affine general linear group acting on 𝔸d​(𝔽q)\mathbb{A}^{d}(\mathbb{F}_{q}); it is an extension of GLd⁡(𝔽q)\operatorname{GL}_{d}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) by the group of translations (𝔽q)d(\mathbb{F}_{q})^{d}. The group A​Γ​Ld⁡(q)\operatorname{A\Gamma L}_{d}(q) is generated by AGLd⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{d}(q) and the Frobenius automorphism. The group PGLd⁡(q)=GLd⁡(q)/𝔽q×\operatorname{PGL}_{d}(q)=\operatorname{GL}_{d}(q)/\mathbb{F}_{q}^{\times} is the projective general linear group acting on the projective space ℙd−1​(𝔽q)\mathbb{P}^{d-1}(\mathbb{F}_{q}). The projective semilinear group P​Γ​Ld⁡(q)\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_{d}(q) is generated by PGLd⁡(q)\operatorname{PGL}_{d}(q) and the Frobenius automorphism.

In Lemma 3.4 we use inertia groups to construct special subgroups of the sectional monodromy group; together Proposition 2.8 and Lemma 3.4 will reduce most of the computation of sectional monodromy groups to pure group theory. First we need to prove the following lemma.

Lemma 3.2.

Let KK be an algebraically closed field of characteristic pp and let (F,v)\left(F,v\right) denote the valued field K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}. Let 𝒪\mathcal{O} denote its ring of integers 𝒪=K⁡[[t]]\mathcal{O}={K[\![t]\!]}. Let P∈𝒪⁡[[x]]P\in\mathcal{O}[\![x]\!] be an arbitrary power series and let qq be a power of pp. Consider a power series Q=xq+2​P​(x)+aq+1​xq+1+aq​xq+a1​x+a0∈𝒪⁡[[x]]Q=x^{q+2}P(x)+a_{q+1}x^{q+1}+a_{q}x^{q}+a_{1}x+a_{0}\in\mathcal{O}[\![x]\!], where v⁡(a0)=v⁡(a1)=1v(a_{0})=v(a_{1})=1, v⁡(aq)=0v(a_{q})=0. Assume that v⁡(a1​aq−a0​aq+1)=1v(a_{1}a_{q}-a_{0}a_{q+1})=1. Assume that all roots of QQ in the open unit disk D:⁣={x∈F¯:v(x)>0}D\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{x\in\overline{F}:\ v(x)>0\} lie in FsepF^{\mathrm{sep}}, so QQ has exactly qq roots in DD. The Galois action on these roots defines a homomorphism φ:Gal⁡(F¯/F)→Sq\varphi\colon\Gal(\overline{F}/F)\to S_{q}. Let HH denote the image of φ\varphi. Then HH equals AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) embedded via its action on the affine line.

Proof.

The Newton polygon of QQ has a unique segment of positive slope, it connects (0,1)(0,1) and (q,0)(q,0). Therefore QQ has qq roots in the open unit disk each with valuation 1/q1/q. Let α\alpha be a root of QQ. The field extension L=F⁡(α)/FL=F(\alpha)/F has ramification index at least qq; therefore [L:F]=q[L:F]=q and HH acts transitively. Consider the roots of Q⁡(x+α)Q(x+\alpha) over LL. We have

Q⁡(x+α)=xq​(x+α)2​P​(x+α)+αq​(x+α)2​P​(x+α)+aq+1​xq​(x+α)+aq+1​αq​(x+α)+aq​xq+a1​x+a1​α+aq​αq+a0.Q(x+\alpha)=x^{q}(x+\alpha)^{2}P(x+\alpha)+\alpha^{q}(x+\alpha)^{2}P(x+\alpha)+a_{q+1}x^{q}(x+\alpha)\\ +a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}(x+\alpha)+a_{q}x^{q}+a_{1}x+a_{1}\alpha+a_{q}\alpha^{q}+a_{0}.

The constant term must be zero since α\alpha is a root of QQ. The constant term of Q⁡(x+α)/xQ(x+\alpha)/x is

2​αq+1​P​(α)+αq+2​P′​(α)+aq+1​αq+a1.2\alpha^{q+1}P(\alpha)+\alpha^{q+2}P^{\prime}(\alpha)+a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}+a_{1}.

Assume v⁡(aq+1​αq+a1)>1v(a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}+a_{1})>1. Then aq+1​αq+a1≡0(modαq+1)a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}+a_{1}\equiv 0\pmod{\alpha^{q+1}}. Reducing the equation Q⁡(α)=0Q(\alpha)=0 modulo αq+1\alpha^{q+1}, we conclude that a0+aq​αq≡0(modαq+1)a_{0}+a_{q}\alpha^{q}\equiv 0\pmod{\alpha^{q+1}}. Hence αq≡−a0/aq(modαq+1)\alpha^{q}\equiv-a_{0}/a_{q}\pmod{\alpha^{q+1}} and a1−a0​aq+1/aq≡aq+1​αq+a1≡0(modαq+1)a_{1}-a_{0}a_{q+1}/a_{q}\equiv a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}+a_{1}\equiv 0\pmod{\alpha^{q+1}}. But v⁡(aq+1​a0/aq−a1)=1v(a_{q+1}a_{0}/a_{q}-a_{1})=1, contradiction. Thus v⁡(aq+1​αq+a1)=1v(a_{q+1}\alpha^{q}+a_{1})=1, and the constant term of Q⁡(x+α)/xQ(x+\alpha)/x has valuation 11.

The power series Q⁡(x+α)/x=:∑kbk​xkQ(x+\alpha)/x=\vcentcolon\sum_{k}b_{k}x^{k} has constant term b0b_{0} of valuation 11. Modulo αq\alpha^{q} we have Q⁡(x+α)/x≡xq−1​(x+α)2​P​(x)+aq+1​xq−1​(x+α)+aq​xq−1(modαq)Q(x+\alpha)/x\equiv x^{q-1}(x+\alpha)^{2}P(x)+a_{q+1}x^{q-1}(x+\alpha)+a_{q}x^{q-1}\pmod{\alpha^{q}}. So for 1⩽k⩽q−21\leqslant k\leqslant q-2 the valuation of bkb_{k} is at least one. The valuation of bq−1b_{q-1} is zero. Therefore the Newton polygon of Q⁡(x+α)/xQ(x+\alpha)/x has only one segment of positive slope, it connects (0,1)(0,1) to (q−1,0)(q-1,0). The field L=K⁡((α))L={K(\!(\alpha)\!)} has a unique extension of degree q−1q-1, namely K⁡((α1/(q−1))){K(\!(\alpha^{1/(q-1)})\!)}. We conclude that the stabilizer of a point in HH is a cyclic group of order (q−1)(q-1). A cycle in an imprimitive group has to either belong to a block or contain the same number of elements in every block. Since q−1q-1 and qq are relatively prime, a (q−1)(q-1)-cycle belongs to a single block. So the group cannot be imprimitive. Since FF is a nonarchimedean local field, HH is solvable. Theorem 3.1 implies that in this case AGL1⁡(q)⊂H⊂A​Γ​L1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q)\subset H\subset\operatorname{A\Gamma L}_{1}(q). The group A​Γ​L1⁡(q)\operatorname{A\Gamma L}_{1}(q) is the group of semilinear transformation of the affine line, namely the group generated by AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) and the Frobenius automorphism. Since the stabilizer of a point in HH is a cyclic group, H=AGL1⁡(q)H=\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q).

∎

Remark 3.3.

Lemma 3.2 can be proved without using Theorem 3.1 with a lengthier but elementary group theory argument. The main Theorems 1.4 and 1.6 rely on Theorem 3.1 in a more substantial way.

Lemma 3.4.

Let X⊂ℙ2X\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} be a nondegenerate nonstrange integral plane curve of degree dd. Assume that the Gauss map of XX has separable degree ss and inseparable degree qq. Choose a geometric point xx above which the covering πX\pi_{X} is étale.     • •

Let U⊂(ℙ2)∗U\subset(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*} be a dense open subset over which the covering πX\pi_{X} is étale. The complement of UU contains finitely many lines. A line in (ℙ2)∗(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*} defines a point in (ℙ2)∗⁣∗=ℙ2(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{**}=\mathbb{P}^{2}. Let S⊂ℙ2S\subset\mathbb{P}^{2} be the set of points corresponding to lines in the complement of UU. Then for every point P∉SP\not\in S the restriction of πX\pi_{X} to the family of lines passing through PP is generically étale. A general tangent to XX is tangent at exactly ss points with multiplicity max⁡(2,q)\max(2,q) at each one. Since XX is not strange, a general tangent line does not intersect the set of singular points SingX\mathrm{Sing}_{X} of XX and does not intersect SS. Choose a line in ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2} that is disjoint from both ⋃iPi\bigcup_{i}P_{i} and ⋃jQj\bigcup_{j}Q_{j}. Consider the affine plane 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} obtained by removing the chosen line. Choose coordinates x,yx,y in 𝔸2\mathbb{A}^{2} so that ℓ\ell is the line y=0y=0, and the coordinates of P1,…,PsP_{1},...,P_{s} are (α1,0),(α2,0),…,(αs,0)(\alpha_{1},0),(\alpha_{2},0),...,(\alpha_{s},0). Choose an algebraic closure of the fraction field of the local ring at [ℓ]∈(ℙ2)∗[\ell]\in(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*}; identify Ω\Omega with the fiber at the geometric point corresponding to this choice. Let Ai⊂ΩA_{i}\subset\Omega be the set that reduces to PiP_{i}, and let B=Ω∖⋃iAiB=\Omega\setminus\bigcup_{i}A_{i} be the rest of Ω\Omega. For an element α∈K\alpha\in K consider the family of lines ℓt=ℓt​(α)\ell_{t}=\ell_{t}(\alpha) given by the equation y=t⁡(x−α)y=t(x-\alpha). The family ℓt​(α)\ell_{t}(\alpha) is the family of lines passing through (α,0)(\alpha,0), so the covering πX\pi_{X} is generically étale above the line corresponding to ℓt​(α)\ell_{t}(\alpha) in (ℙ2)∗(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*}. We want to analyze inertia groups at t=0t=0 of the restriction of πX\pi_{X} to these families.

  1. (1)

    Assume q=1q=1. In this case char⁡K≠2\Char K\neq 2, see [Katz1973]*Proposition 3.3. We need to describe the extension of K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)} obtained by adjoining the coordinates of the intersection of XX with y=t⁡(x−α)y=t(x-\alpha). Choose a uniformizer xi=x−αix_{i}=x-\alpha_{i}. Similarly, if α=αi\alpha=\alpha_{i} the equation Qi=0Q_{i}=0 has two positively valued roots, both lying in K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}. Taking α\alpha to be distinct from each αi\alpha_{i} gives an element g∈GXg\in G_{X} that fixes BB and acts on each AiA_{i} as a transposition. Taking α=α1\alpha=\alpha_{1} gives an element g1∈GXg_{1}\in G_{X} that acts by identity on B∪A1B\cup A_{1} and as a transposition on AjA_{j} for all j≠1j\neq 1. The product g​g1gg_{1} is a transposition.

    Now assume q>1q>1 is a power of the characteristic. This statement is similar to part (1), except the degrees of the extensions are no longer 22 and some wild ramification appears. Let (xi,pi​(xi))(x_{i},p_{i}(x_{i})) be the uniformization and define ci,dic_{i},d_{i} by pi​(xi)=di​xq+ci​xq+1+O⁡(xq+1)p_{i}(x_{i})=d_{i}x^{q}+c_{i}x^{q+1}+O(x^{q+1}). The xx-coordinates of the intersection points that reduce to PiP_{i} are the positively valued roots of Qi​(x)=pi​(xi)−t​xi+t⁡(α−αi)Q_{i}(x)=p_{i}(x_{i})-tx_{i}+t(\alpha-\alpha_{i}). Remark 3.5.

When char⁡K=0\Char K=0 Lemmas 3.4 and 2.2 imply that GG is 22-transitive and contains a transposition, so G=SdG=S_{d}.

4. Sectional monodromy groups of nonstrange curves

The main result of this section is Theorem 4.5 that describes sectional monodromy groups of nonstrange space curves. The sectional monodromy group of a nonstrange space curve is triply transitive by Proposition 2.8. Triply transitive permutation groups can be classified; for a statement and definitions of relevant groups see [Cameron1999]*Sections 7.3, 7.4.

Proposition 4.1.

If GG is a triply transitive permutation group of degree dd then either G⊃AdG\supset A_{d} or one of the following holds.

  1. (1)

    G=AGLn⁡(2)G=\operatorname{AGL}_{n}(2), d=2nd=2^{n};

  2. (2)

    G=G1G=G_{1}, d=16d=16;

  3. (3)

    PSL2⁡(r)⊂G⊂P​Γ​L2⁡(r)\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(r)\subset G\subset\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_{2}(r), d=r+1d=r+1, rr is a power of a prime;

  4. (4)

    G=M11G=M_{11}, d=11d=11;

  5. (5)

    G=M11G=M_{11}, d=12d=12;

  6. (6)

    G=M12G=M_{12}, d=12d=12

  7. (7)

    G=M22G=M_{22}, d=22d=22;

  8. (8)

    G=Aut⁡(M22)G=\Aut(M_{22}), d=22d=22;

  9. (9)

    G=M23G=M_{23}, d=23d=23;

  10. (10)

    G=M24G=M_{24}, d=24d=24.

Remark 4.2.

The group G1G_{1} is a subgroup of AGL4⁡(2)\operatorname{AGL}_{4}(2). It is a semidirect product of the translation group 𝔽24\mathbb{F}_{2}^{4} and a specially embedded copy of A7⊂GL4⁡(2)≃A8A_{7}\subset\operatorname{GL}_{4}(2)\simeq A_{8}.

We will also need two geometric statements before proving Theorem 4.5.

Proposition 4.3 (Kaji).

Let X⊂ℙrX\subset\mathbb{P}^{r}, r⩾3r\geqslant 3 be a projective integral nonstrange curve, let γX:X→X∗\upgamma_{X}\colon X\to X^{*} be its Gauss map. Let Y⊂ℙr−1Y\subset\mathbb{P}^{r-1} be the projection of XX from a general point P∈ℙrP\in\mathbb{P}^{r}. Identify K⁡(X)K(X) and K⁡(Y)K(Y) via the projection from PP. Let γY:Y→Y∗\upgamma_{Y}\colon Y\to Y^{*} denote the Gauss map of YY. Then the subfield K⁡(X∗)K(X^{*}) of K⁡(X)K(X) defined by γX\upgamma_{X} and the subfield K⁡(Y∗)K(Y^{*}) of K⁡(X)=K⁡(Y)K(X)=K(Y) defined by γY:Y\upgamma_{Y}\colon Y coincide.

Proof.

See [Kaji1989]*Theorem 2.1 and the remark following the theorem. ∎

Proposition 4.4 ([Ballico-Cossidente1999]*Theorem 3.1).

Let X⊂ℙ3X\subset\mathbb{P}^{3} be a smooth curve of degree dd. Assume that for a general point PP of XX there is no tangent line to XX at a point Q≠PQ\neq P that intersects the tangent line at PP. Then either d=3d=3 and XX is a twisted cubic or d=q+1d=q+1 for some power qq of the characteristic. In the latter case XX is rational and isomorphic to the projective closure of the parametrized curve (t,tq,tq+1)(t,t^{q},t^{q+1}).

The following theorem is the main result of this section.

Theorem 4.5.

Let X⊂ℙmX\subset\mathbb{P}^{m}, m⩾3m\geqslant 3 be a nondegenerate integral nonstrange curve of degree dd. Then one of the following holds.

  1. (1)

    The sectional monodromy group GG contains the alternating group AdA_{d}.

  2. (2)

    m=3m=3 and XX is projectively equivalent to the rational curve given as the projective closure of the parametrized curve (t,tq,tq+1)⊂𝔸3(t,t^{q},t^{q+1})\subset\mathbb{A}^{3} for some power qq of the characteristic. In this case G=PGL2⁡(q)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(q).

  3. (3)

    m=3m=3, char⁡K=2\Char K=2, the tangent variety of XX is a smooth quadric and GG is contained in AGLn⁡(2)\operatorname{AGL}_{n}(2).

Proof.

Let s,qs,q be the separable and inseparable degrees of the Gauss map γX\upgamma_{X} of XX. Recall that for a general tangent line ℓ\ell of XX the degree of the scheme-theoretic intersection of XX and ℓ\ell satisfies deg⁡X∩ℓ=deg⁡γ=s​q\deg X\cap\ell=\deg\upgamma=sq. Choose one such general tangent line ℓ\ell and choose a point PP of XX that does not lie on ℓ\ell. Let HH be a hyperplane containing ℓ\ell and PP. The degree of the intersection of HH with XX satisfies d=deg⁡X=deg⁡H∩X⩾deg⁡ℓ∩X+1=s​q+1d=\deg X=\deg H\cap X\geqslant\deg\ell\cap X+1=sq+1. Therefore s​q<dsq<d.

By Proposition 4.3 ss and qq are also the separable and inseparable degrees of a general projection of XX. Let X′X^{\prime} be a general projection of XX to ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}. Proposition 2.10 implies that GX=GX′G_{X}=G_{X^{\prime}} as permutation groups. Since X′X^{\prime} is a plane curve, Lemma 3.4 applies. We conclude that if q=1q=1 the group GG contains a transposition, and therefore G=SnG=S_{n}. Assume q>1q>1 and fix a decomposition Ω=A1⊔…⊔As⊔B\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup...\sqcup A_{s}\sqcup B, subgroups H,Hi⊂GH,H_{i}\subset G, and an element h∈Hh\in H as in Lemma 3.4. We will use the properties of (Ai,B,Hi,H,h)(A_{i},B,H_{i},H,h) stated in Lemma 3.4 throughout this proof. Since s​q<dsq<d the set BB is nonempty.

The group GG is triply transitive by Proposition 2.8. Therefore it is on the list of Proposition 4.1. We analyze each possibility.

  1. Case (a):

    G⊂AGLn⁡(2)G\subset\operatorname{AGL}_{n}(2) and Ω=𝔽2n\Omega=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}. This case also covers the G1G_{1} group of Proposition 4.1, since G1G_{1} is a permutation subgroup of AGL4⁡(2)\operatorname{AGL}_{4}(2). Assume first that q≠2q\neq 2. The element h∈Gh\in G acts as a product of ss (q−1)(q-1)-cycles. The element hh has a fixed point, which we may assume is the origin in 𝔽2n\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n}, so h∈GLn⁡(𝔽2)h\in\operatorname{GL}_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{2}). Consider Ω=𝔽2n\Omega=\mathbb{F}_{2}^{n} as an 𝔽2​[t]\mathbb{F}_{2}[t] module, where tt acts as hh. Since hh has fixed points and is not equal to the identity, one of the following cases holds.

    1. (i)

      Ω\Omega has a submodule WW isomorphic to 𝔽2​[t]/(t−1)n\mathbb{F}_{2}[t]/(t-1)^{n} for some n>1n>1. Let MM be the restriction of hh to WW. Then Mq−1−1=0M^{q-1}-1=0. So tq−1−1t^{q-1}-1 is divisible by (t−1)n(t-1)^{n} in 𝔽2​[t]\mathbb{F}_{2}[t], therefore n⩽v2​(q−1)n\leqslant v_{2}(q-1). This implies that the number of points in WW is 2n⩽q−12^{n}\leqslant q-1. But q−1q-1 is the minimal size of a nontrivial orbit of hh, contradiction.

    2. (ii)

      Ω=V1⊕V2\Omega=V_{1}\oplus V_{2}, where V1≠0V_{1}\neq 0 is indecomposable and V2V_{2} contains all nonzero fixed points of hh. Then for every fixed point vv of hh, v+V1v+V_{1} is invariant under the action of hh. Therefore, hh has at least as many orbits of length greater than 11 as it has fixed points. On the other hand, since hh acts on AiA_{i} via fixing one point and permuting the rest cyclically and also fixes B≠∅B\neq\emptyset pointwise, AA has more fixed points than it has orbits of length greater than one. Contradiction.

    Assume q=2q=2. The set BB is the set of common fixed points of the elements of HH. Therefore BB forms an affine space, and #​B\#B is a power of 22. Similarly B∪A1B\cup A_{1} is the set of common fixed points of elements of H1H_{1}. Therefore #​B+#​A1=#​B+2\#B+\#A_{1}=\#B+2 is a power of 22. Hence #​B=2\#B=2, and 2n=#​Ω=2​s+#​B2^{n}=\#\Omega=2s+\#B, so s=2n−1−1s=2^{n-1}-1. We can assume that the tangent variety of XX is not a quadric, since otherwise we are in case (3). If n=2n=2, then a nonidentity element of HH acts on Ω\Omega as a transposition, hence G=SdG=S_{d}. Suppose n>2n>2. Then XX has degree 2n>42^{n}>4 and therefore XX lies on at most one quadric surface. For a general tangent line ℓ\ell of XX there does not exist a quadric QQ containing XX and ℓ\ell. Consider a triple ℓ1,ℓ2,ℓ3\ell_{1},\ell_{2},\ell_{3} of general tangents to XX. Remark 4.6.

Suppose char⁡K≠2\Char K\neq 2. Then the group GG is contained in the alternating group if and only if the separability degree of the Gauss map is even [Rathmann1987]*Theorem 2.10. When char⁡K=2\Char K=2 we do not know under what conditions GG is equal to SnS_{n}.

5. Galois groups of trinomials

In this section we study the Galois group GG of the polynomial xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b over the field K⁡(a,b)K(a,b). The following theorem of Cohen covers most of the previously known results about GG.

Theorem 5.1 ([Cohen1980]*Corollary 3).

Assume that nn and mm are relatively prime, p∤m⁡(n−m)p\nmid m(n-m) and if m=1m=1 or m=n−1m=n-1 assume additionally that p∤np\nmid n. Then An⊂GA_{n}\subset G. Moreover, if pp is odd, then G=SnG=S_{n}.

Some cases not covered by Theorem 5.1, such as a trinomial with G=M11G=M_{11}, are described in [Uchida1970]. Our goal is to compute all the possibilities for GG.

We begin by fixing notation. Throughout this section, (n,m)(n,m) is a pair of relatively prime positive integers, Xn,mX_{n,m} denotes the projective rational curve plane xn=ym​zn−mx^{n}=y^{m}z^{n-m}, and G=Gn,mG=G_{n,m} is the sectional monodromy group of Xn,mX_{n,m}. An affine parametrization of Xn,mX_{n,m} is (tm,tn)(t^{m},t^{n}). Therefore GG is also the Galois group of the trinomial xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b over K⁡(a,b)K(a,b). Without loss of generality we assume that m<n/2m<n/2 since Xn,m≃Xn,n−mX_{n,m}\simeq X_{n,n-m}.

We start by describing properties of tangent lines and Gauss maps of the curves Xn,mX_{n,m}.

Proposition 5.2.
  1. (1)

    If n,mn,m and (n−m)(n-m) are prime to pp, then Xn,mX_{n,m} is nonstrange. In this case the Gauss map has separability degree 11, and inseparability degree 11 when p>2p>2 and 22 when p=2p=2.

  2. (2)

    Assume that k∈{n,m,n−m}k\in\{n,m,n-m\} is divisible by pp. Write k=q​dk=qd where qq is the largest power of pp that divides kk. Then Xn,mX_{n,m} is strange and the Gauss map has inseparability degree qq and separability degree dd.

p⁡(X)=(Z+αm)n−(nm​αn−m​Z+αn)m.p(X)=(Z+\alpha^{m})^{n}-\left(\frac{n}{m}\alpha^{n-m}Z+\alpha^{n}\right)^{m}.

(n⁡(n−1)2−n⁡(m−1)2)​αm⁡(n−2).\left(\frac{n(n-1)}{2}-\frac{n(m-1)}{2}\right)\alpha^{m(n-2)}.

This coefficient is identically zero if and only if either p|np|n or p|(n−m)p|(n-m).

    p∤n,p∤n−mp\nmid n,p\nmid n-m. In this case the inseparability degree of the Gauss map is 11. We can recover the point (αn,αm)(\alpha^{n},\alpha^{m}) from its tangent line

We now prove a stronger version of Lemma 3.4 for curves Xn,mX_{n,m}.

Lemma 5.3.

Let X=Xn,mX=X_{n,m} be one of the trinomial curves. Choose a geometric point δ\delta of (ℙ2)∗(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*} above which the covering πX\pi_{X} is étale. Denote by Ω\Omega the fiber of πX\pi_{X} above δ\delta, so the group G=GXG=G_{X} acts on Ω\Omega by permutations. Then the following hold.

  1. (1)

    Assume p|np|n. Write n=q​dn=qd with qq a power of pp and dd prime to pp. Then there exists a decomposition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ad\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup...\sqcup A_{d}, a subgroup H⊂GH\subset G, a collection of subgrops Hi⊂GH_{i}\subset G, i=1,…,di=1,...,d, and an element h∈Hh\in H with the following properties.

    • •

      For every ii the set AiA_{i} is of cardinality qq.

    • •

      The image of HH in Sym⁡(Ai)\mathrm{Sym}(A_{i}) equals AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) embedded via its action on 𝔸1​(𝔽q)\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

    • •

      The element h∈Hh\in H acts on each AiA_{i} with one fixed point and one orbit of size q−1q-1.

    • •

      The group HiH_{i} acts on AiA_{i} with one fixed point and one orbit of size q−1q-1. The image of HiH_{i} in Sym⁡(Aj)\mathrm{Sym}(A_{j}) for i≠ji\neq j contains AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) embedded via its action on 𝔸1​(𝔽q)\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

  2. (2)

    Assume p|n−mp|n-m. Write n−m=q​dn-m=qd with qq a power of pp and dd prime to pp. Then there exists a decomposition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ad⊔B\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup...\sqcup A_{d}\sqcup B, a subgroup H⊂GH\subset G, a collection of subgrops Hi⊂GH_{i}\subset G, i=1,…,di=1,...,d, and an element h∈Hh\in H with the following properties.

    • •

      For every ii the set AiA_{i} is of cardinality qq.

    • •

      The image of HH in Sym⁡(Ai)\mathrm{Sym}(A_{i}) equals AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) embedded via its action on 𝔸1​(𝔽q)\mathbb{A}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{q}).

    • •

      The element h∈Hh\in H acts on each AiA_{i} with one fixed point and one orbit of size q−1q-1.

    • •

      The image of HH in Sym⁡(B)\mathrm{Sym}(B) is ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z} in its natural embedding; hh maps to a generator of ℤ/m​ℤ\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}.

Proof.

Both parts of the statement are proved similarly to Lemma 3.4. We will pick a tangent line ℓ\ell to Xn,mX_{n,m}. We will then restrict the covering to a family of lines that includes ℓ\ell and compute the inertia group at [ℓ]∈(ℙ2)∗[\ell]\in(\mathbb{P}^{2})^{*}. To calculate the inertia groups we will use Lemma 3.2 and a computation of local uniformization.

  1. (1)

    Replacing KK with a larger algebraically closed field if necessary, we can choose an element u∈Ku\in K that is not a root of unity. Consider the affine model xn=ymx^{n}=y^{m} of XX. Let xi=x−αix_{i}=x-\alpha_{i}. Theorem 5.4.

Suppose mm and nn are relatively prime integers satisfying m⩽n/2m\leqslant n/2. Let GG be the Galois group of the polynomial P(x):⁣=xn+axm+bP(x)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}x^{n}+ax^{m}+b over K⁡(a,b)K(a,b), and let p=char⁡Kp=\Char K.

  1. (1)

    If m=1m=1 and n=pdn=p^{d}, then G=AGL1⁡(pd)G=\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(p^{d}).

  2. (2)

    If m=1m=1, n=6n=6, and p=2p=2, then G=PSL2⁡(5)G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(5).

  3. (3)

    If m=1m=1, n=12n=12, and p=3p=3, then G=M11G=M_{11}.

  4. (4)

    If m=1m=1, n=24n=24, and p=2p=2, then G=M24G=M_{24}.

  5. (5)

    If m=2m=2, n=11n=11, and p=3p=3, then G=M11G=M_{11}.

  6. (6)

    If m=3m=3, n=23n=23, and p=2p=2, then G=M23G=M_{23}.

  7. (7)

    Let q:⁣=pkq\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}p^{k} for some kk. If n=(qd−1)/(q−1)n=(q^{d}-1)/(q-1), m=(qs−1)/(q−1)m=(q^{s}-1)/(q-1) for some s,ds,d, then G=PGLd⁡(q)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{d}(q).

  8. (8)

    If none of the above holds, then An⊂GA_{n}\subset G.

Proof.

We break the proof into cases corresponding to the cases of Proposition 5.2. The case n=2n=2 is trivial. In what follows we assume n>2n>2 so that m<n/2m<n/2 since m,nm,n are relatively prime.

  1. (1)

    Assume p∤n​m​(n−m)p\nmid nm(n-m). By Proposition 5.2 the curve Xm,nX_{m,n} is nonstrange and the Gauss map is either birational or purely inseparable of degree two. In any case Lemma 3.4 implies that GG contains a transposition; hence G=SnG=S_{n}.

  2. (2)

    Assume p|np|n. Consider the specialization of xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b to the polynomial P(x):⁣=xn+t−1xm+1P(x)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}x^{n}+t^{-1}x^{m}+1 over the field K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}. The Newton polygon of PP consists of two segments: one from (0,0)(0,0) to (m,−1)(m,-1) and one from (m,−1)(m,-1) to (n,0)(n,0). Since n−mn-m and mm are relatively prime and are both prime to pp, the group GG contains an mm-cycle and an (n−m)(n-m)-cycle. If m≠1m\neq 1, then An⊂GA_{n}\subset G by Theorem 3.1. If m=1m=1 and An⊄GA_{n}\not\subset G, then Theorem 3.1 implies that one of the following holds

    1. (1)

      n=pdn=p^{d} . In this case the Galois group is AGL1⁡(pd)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(p^{d}), see [Rathmann1987]*Example 2.17.

    2. (2)

      n=ℓ+1n=\ell+1 for some prime ℓ\ell and G=PSL2⁡(ℓ)G=\operatorname{PSL}_{2}(\ell) or G=PGL2⁡(ℓ)G=\operatorname{PGL}_{2}(\ell). If d=1d=1, then nn is a power of pp, which is precisely the case (2)(1) above. Assume d>1d>1. Lemma 5.3 applies in this case with B=∅B=\emptyset. There is a unique such element, namely multiplication by −1-1. In particular g1g_{1} acts as a transposition on AiA_{i} for i>1i>1. Take an element g2∈Hg_{2}\in H that acts on A1A_{1} as a transposition. If d⩾4d\geqslant 4, then either g2g_{2} or g1​g2g_{1}g_{2} fixes at least four points, contradiction. If d=2d=2, then g1g_{1} acts a transposition and so G=SnG=S_{n}. If d=3d=3, then ℓ=5\ell=5 (and q=2q=2). Suppose ℓ=5\ell=5, q=2q=2. There is a factorization

      x6+a​x+b=(x3+c​x2+c2​α​x+ac2+α​c3)​(x3+c​x2+(c2​α+c2)​x+ac2+(α+1)​c3),x^{6}+ax+b=\left(x^{3}+cx^{2}+c^{2}\alpha x+\frac{a}{c^{2}}+\alpha c^{3}\right)\left(x^{3}+cx^{2}+(c^{2}\alpha+c^{2})x+\frac{a}{c^{2}}+(\alpha+1)c^{3}\right),

      Suppose p=3p=3. Let G^\widehat{G} denote the Galois group of P⁡(x)P(x) over 𝔽9​(a,b)\mathbb{F}_{9}(a,b).     Assume p|mp|m. Consider the specialization of xn+a​xm+bx^{n}+ax^{m}+b to the polynomial P⁡(x)=xn+tP(x)=x^{n}+t over K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}.   4. (4)

    Assume p|n−mp|n-m. Consider the specialization xn+tx^{n}+t over K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}. Since n,mn,m are relatively prime, the specialized polynomial is separable with cyclic Galois group.     1. (1)

      Cℓ⊂G⊂AGL1⁡(ℓ)C_{\ell}\subset G\subset\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(\ell), n=ℓ⩾5n=\ell\geqslant 5 is prime. Consider the specialization xn+t−1​xm+1x^{n}+t^{-1}x^{m}+1 over K⁡((t)){K(\!(t)\!)}. Any element from the wild inertia subgroup fixes at least mm roots. Therefore m=1m=1. In this case Lemma 5.3 applies with #​B=1\#B=1. The stabilizer of BB in G⊂AGL1⁡(ℓ)G\subset\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(\ell) is abelian and has AGL1⁡(q)\operatorname{AGL}_{1}(q) as a subquotient, thus q=2q=2. Since ℓ⩾5\ell\geqslant 5 the group H1H_{1} has an element g≠i​dg\neq id. The element gg fixes at least two points, contradiction.

    2. (2)

      PGLr⁡(ℓ)⊂G⊂P​Γ​Lr⁡(ℓ)\operatorname{PGL}_{r}(\ell)\subset G\subset\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_{r}(\ell), n=#​ℙr−1​(𝔽ℓ)=(ℓr−1)/(ℓ−1)n=\#\mathbb{P}^{r-1}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell})=(\ell^{r}-1)/(\ell-1). We will prove that ℓ\ell is necessarily a power of pp and that m=#​ℙr′​(𝔽ℓ)m=\#\mathbb{P}^{r^{\prime}}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell}) for some r′<rr^{\prime}<r.

      We can assume that PGLr⁡(ℓ)⊅An\operatorname{PGL}_{r}(\ell)\not\supset A_{n}. We call a point blue if it is in the set BB and azure if it is in one of the AiA_{i}’s. Lemma 5.3 implies that for every pair of points P,Q∈AiP,Q\in A_{i} there is an element of GG that fixes all blue points and moves PP to QQ. Our goal is to show that p|ℓp|\ell and BB forms a projective subspace of Ω\Omega. To this end we examine the Galois action on lines that contain blue points.

      Consider a line ll in ℙr​(𝔽ℓ)\mathbb{P}^{r}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell}) that contains at least 33 blue points; identify this line with ℙ1​(𝔽ℓ)\mathbb{P}^{1}(\mathbb{F}_{\ell}). Any element of GG that fixes all blue points is a power of the Frobenius when restricted to ll. Since any azure point can be moved by an element of GG that fixes all blue points, the set of blue points of ll is the set l⁡(𝔽t)l(\mathbb{F}_{t}) for some subfield 𝔽t⊂𝔽ℓ\mathbb{F}_{t}\subset\mathbb{F}_{\ell}. There is a subgroup of HH that fixes all blue points and acts transitively on AiA_{i} for every ii. Thus if ll contains a point from AiA_{i}, then it contains the whole set AiA_{i}. Assume Ai,Aj⊂lA_{i},A_{j}\subset l for some i≠ji\neq j. The group HiH_{i} fixes all blue points and AiA_{i}, and acts transitively on the rest of the line. Remark 5.5.

Theorem 5.4 does not distinguish between the cases G=AnG=A_{n} and G=SnG=S_{n}, but it is possible to do so. When pp is odd this is discussed in Remark 4.6. If p=2p=2 and nn is even, then G⊂AnG\subset A_{n} by [Abhyankar-Oun-Avinash1994]*Proposition 2.24. If p=2p=2 and nn is odd, then G⊂AnG\subset A_{n} if and only if m=2m=2 by [Abhyankar-Oun-Avinash1994]*Proposition 2.23.
